capabilities.target: chat reply to the authenticated requester
arbitrary public web URL chosen by the model

inputs.source: Jira tickets via planned Jira MCP server, including tickets filed by customers

instructions.note: The instruction 'Answer engineering questions using docs.search' does not state which employees may query. If docs-qa is available to all SSO-authenticated employees rather than only engineers, employees without direct read access to the confidential design docs could obtain their content via chat, bypassing document-level permissions. The artifacts do not confirm the intended audience.

The only control against secret or credential leakage is the prompt rule 'Never paste secrets or credentials into answers.' It is behavioral and dependent, and it only constrains visible chat answer text; it does not address secrets embedded in tool-call arguments such as a URL passed to the planned web.fetch tool. Impact is low today because no egress capability exists, but the rule does not close that gap once web.fetch is added (see forecast finding).

controls.name: SSO authentication for employee chat sessions
Chat client does not render images or fetch links
Engineering design docs are write-restricted to engineers
Prompt rule: never paste secrets or credentials into answers
controls.decay_rationale: A more capable model can rationalize including sensitive snippets it judges necessary, or encode them in non-obvious forms that still satisfy a literal reading of the rule. It also does not cover secrets embedded in tool-call arguments such as URLs.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for web.fetch destinations
Trust labeling and sanitization of Jira ticket content before tool argument construction
controls.decay_rationale: A content-based sanitizer or classifier can be degraded by multi-document or multi-turn payload splitting once the model is more capable at reconstructing instructions from fragments.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action review) for web.fetch calls derived from untrusted content
Tamper-evident audit log attributing agent actions to the requester
Rate or step limit on docs-qa tool calls

findings.title: Forecast: lethal trifecta from planned web.fetch and Jira customer tickets (TC1)

attack_path.note: Untrusted content, including tickets filed by customers, enters the agent's context via the planned Jira MCP server.
Agent reads confidential engineering design docs while composing an answer.
Planned web.fetch tool lets the model choose an outbound URL, enabling exfiltration of the docs content just read via query parameters or path segments.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

evidence.locator: runtime notes: Roadmap for next sprint
evidence.observation: The design states a plan to add a web.fetch tool for public references and a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers; neither exists yet, so no complete path from an untrusted source to an egress sink exists today.

Current instructions only reference docs.search and a rule against pasting secrets into answers; nothing addresses URL/egress restrictions or treatment of ticket content as untrusted, so no control is positioned to cover the new capabilities once added.

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest or MCP client config diff adding a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server entry, without an accompanying egress allowlist or untrusted-content handling for ticket data.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, add a network egress allowlist restricting destinations to a small set of approved public documentation domains, so confidential content read via docs_search cannot be exfiltrated through attacker-chosen URLs.

Treat all content from the Jira MCP server, especially tickets filed by customers, as untrusted input; sanitize or spotlight it before it can influence tool call arguments such as the URL passed to web.fetch.
Add a human approval gate with raw action review for any web.fetch call whose URL argument was influenced by Jira ticket content, until the egress allowlist is proven sufficient.

findings.title: No attributable audit trail for docs-qa actions (property)

evidence.observation: Runtime notes describe SSO authentication and reply restriction to the requester, but do not mention any logging or audit trail tying docs_search or chat_reply actions to the requester's identity.

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch or the Jira MCP server added to the manifest without a corresponding tamper-evident log of agent actions and the data they touched.

recommendations.action: Add tamper-evident logging that attributes each docs_search query and chat_reply to the authenticated employee, especially before any egress-capable tool such as the planned web.fetch is added.

findings.title: No spend, rate, or step limit on docs-qa tool calls (property)

evidence.observation: No mention of rate limiting, step limits, or quotas for docs_search or chat_reply calls anywhere in the artifacts.

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch or the Jira MCP server added without an accompanying step count, rate, or spend cap on tool calls.

recommendations.action: Add a step/rate limit, and once web.fetch exists a request quota, to docs-qa tool calls to bound cost and prevent slow repeated exfiltration attempts from going unnoticed.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent runs as a single internal service behind the org's SSO-authenticated chat client; there is no mechanism in this design by which an external party could spoof the agent's identity to employees.
Artifacts do not describe deployment or integrity controls (e.g., config management, prompt pinning) for the agent process itself.

Artifacts do not state whether docs-qa is restricted to engineers or available to all employees; if broadly available, confidential design doc content could reach employees without underlying document access.
Same scope gap as the agent's own information_disclosure entry: artifacts don't confirm whether docs-qa restricts queries to users with legitimate access to the underlying confidential docs.
No external cost or availability constraint is associated with reading this internal store; resource exhaustion risk is already captured at the agent process level, not specific to the store itself.
The planned Jira MCP server's authentication and identity verification method is not yet specified in the artifacts.
Audit logging for the planned Jira integration is not described.
No rate limiting or quota information for the planned Jira MCP connection is given.
Credential scope for the planned Jira MCP server is not specified in the artifacts.
Whether customer identity on Jira tickets is verified, for example an authenticated portal versus anonymous email-to-ticket, is not stated.
No information on whether customer ticket submissions are attributably logged by the ticketing system.

This is an inbound flow carrying ticket content into the agent; it does not itself carry confidential internal data outward, so it is not a disclosure vector in its own right. The disclosure risk arises later via cap.web_fetch, captured on that flow instead.
Planned Jira integration's message volume and rate limiting are not described.
Transport integrity protections, such as TLS and certificate validation, for the planned web.fetch tool are not described.
Rate limiting or cost caps for the planned web.fetch tool are not described.

The destination of web.fetch is attacker-influenced by design (an arbitrary URL); there is no fixed peer identity to spoof, since the risk here is disclosure to an uncontrolled destination rather than impersonation of a known peer.
No information on logging of outbound destinations once web.fetch is implemented.

rating.rationale: No present-day attack path exceeds low: the only two deployed capabilities (read-only docs search and reply-only chat) are non-egress, non-consequential, and reach only the authenticated requester, with no complete path from an untrusted source to a sensitive sink today. The roadmap item to add a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server that ingests customer-filed tickets would, if deployed without additional controls, open a lethal-trifecta path (untrusted ticket content, a confidential document read, and arbitrary egress) that computes to critical, driven by the absence of any egress allowlist or untrusted-content handling for the new capabilities (new_tool, new_mcp_server triggers). Two property findings, a missing audit trail and missing rate/step limits, are rated low today because the affected capabilities are not consequential, but their projected risk also rises once the planned capabilities land, which is why rating.forecast is driven by ctrl.egress_allowlist_missing's absence rather than by any currently declared control decaying.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No MCP config or tool manifest was provided for docs.search; its scope is inferred from the runtime notes alone (medium confidence).

The artifacts do not state whether docs-qa is restricted to engineers or available to all employees; this affects whether confidential design-doc content could reach employees without direct access to the underlying documents (see the unbounded_scope instructions finding).

The planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are described only at the roadmap level; no destination, authentication, or rate-limit details are available, so the forecast finding's projected risk uses the rubric's reasonable worst-case defaults for an added egress capability and an added untrusted peer.
